title: Estimating Dimensionality of Neural Representations from Finite Samples
claim: Naive dimensionality estimates are strongly biased at small sample sizes, while the proposed corrected estimator recovers the true value regardless of sample count.
layout: 2 line plots side by side with shared legend at right; log x-axes
description: Two side-by-side line plots share a y-axis label gamma (0 to 50) and a legend on the right. The left plot varies the number of stimuli P on a log x-axis from about 20 to 1000. The right plot varies the number of neurons Q on a log x-axis over the same range. A thick translucent blue horizontal band at 50 marks the true dimensionality. A black circle curve (naive) and a green right-pointing triangle curve (row) rise from about 13 up to about 38 and 48 as samples grow. A green left-pointing triangle curve (col) is flat near 40 on the left plot and near 33 on the right plot. A red x curve (both) stays on the blue true line near 50 at every sample size. The eye goes first to the red line sitting on the blue line, above the biased curves.
caption: Different dimensionality estimates of the linear model with $d=50$ and noise variance $\sigma^2_\epsilon=0.2$. Left: varying number of stimuli $P$ with fixed $Q=100$ neurons. Right: varying number of neurons $Q$ with fixed $P=200$ stimuli. The horizontal line marks the true dimensionality $\gamma=d=50$.
abstract: The global dimensionality of a neural representation manifold provides rich insight into the computational process underlying both artificial and biological neural networks. However, all existing measures of global dimensionality are sensitive to the number of samples, i.e., the number of rows and columns of the sample matrix. We show that, in particular, the participation ratio of eigenvalues, a popular measure of global dimensionality, is highly biased with small sample sizes, and propose a bias-corrected estimator that is more accurate with finite samples and with noise. On synthetic data examples, we demonstrate that our estimator can recover the true known dimensionality. We apply our estimator to neural brain recordings, including calcium imaging, electrophysiological recordings, and fMRI data, and to the neural activations in a large language model and show our estimator is invariant to the sample size. Finally, our estimators can additionally be used to measure the local dimensionalities of curved neural manifolds by weighting the finite samples appropriately.
